design_detail: Systematic review (PRISMA; PROSPERO CRD42021233519) of interactions between psychiatric medicines and MDMA or psilocybin, written as a narrative synthesis: no pooled estimate and no risk-of-bias rating of the included studies. One database (MEDLINE via PubMed), English only, 1958 to 21 December 2020; 163 title-or-abstract terms (22 medication-class terms, 135 medicine names, 6 MDMA or psilocybin terms) with 21 publication-type and human filters gave 455 records; 12 more were added by hand. Flow (Fig. 1): 467 screened, 411 excluded on title or abstract, 56 read in full, 16 excluded (no reasons given), 40 included: 26 trial publications, 3 epidemiologic studies and 11 case reports that are summarized only in a supplement. The 26 trial publications are 17 original trials plus 9 secondary or exploratory analyses of the same samples; 22 are on MDMA (13 distinct trials in Table 5) and 4 on psilocybin. Each trial compared a medicine plus MDMA with placebo plus MDMA, and the review expresses the difference as a percent change by a formula it gives in Methods.
can_establish: What was found, under controlled laboratory conditions, when one dose or a short course of a psychiatric medicine was given before MDMA to healthy adults: the direction and rough size (as the review computes them, with no intervals) of changes in blood levels of MDMA and its metabolites, vital signs and ratings of effects, for adrenergic, antipsychotic, antidepressant (SSRI, SNRI, noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor, bupropion), stimulant and NMDA-antagonist medicines, and which classes have no controlled data at all.
cannot_establish: How people who take a medicine for months or years, with the illness it treats, respond to MDMA (every trial used healthy adults given the medicine once or for at most 14 days); whether any combination is safe or dangerous outside the laboratory (no trial measured serotonin toxicity, seizures or death, and street MDMA of unknown content is not covered); how large or precise any effect is (percent changes without intervals, some read off graphs, no risk-of-bias rating); anything controlled about MAOIs, benzodiazepines or lithium with MDMA; or causal effects from the surveillance database, the survey and the case reports.

sample.recruitment: Database search of MEDLINE only; 12 of the 40 included publications (30%, editors' calculation) were found by hand, including two (Cohen et al., 2021; Nayak et al., 2021) published after the search date (Study selection, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Results, 1st paragraph). The trial samples were healthy adults, often recruited on university campuses, with 8 to 23 participants per trial in the text (Results, 2nd paragraph); the surveillance study analysed 946 reports, the survey 216 adults and the online-reports analysis 96 accounts (Results > Epidemiologic studies).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: human studies in English, any age, any design (meta-analyses, systematic reviews, randomized trials, retrospective, cross-sectional, case-control and cohort studies, case reports) of a psychiatric medicine taken with MDMA or psilocybin, with outcomes in pharmacokinetics, physiology or subjective effects (Methods, 1st paragraph). Excluded: editorials, duplicates, non-English records and records not addressing the question; 16 full texts were excluded without stated reasons (Fig. 1). Outside the scope by the authors' choice: repeated dosing of MDMA itself, other psychedelics, ketamine (no studies found) and non-psychiatric medicines (Discussion > Limitations). Trial exclusion criteria the authors call common: pregnancy or nursing, age under 18 or over 45, body mass index outside 18.5-25, psychiatric illness in the person or a first-degree relative, and active substance use (Results, 2nd paragraph).
sample.demographics: Of the 13 MDMA trials in Table 5, 11 included women (4 to 8 per trial) and 2 (pindolol, paroxetine) were men only; mean ages 22.9 to 27.4. Previous ecstasy experience ranged from none (duloxetine trial, all ecstasy-naive) through 1 to 6 of 14 or 16 people in eight trials to a mean of 18.8 occasions (memantine), a mean of 28.6 occasions (fluoxetine; the only trial that recruited people who use MDMA recreationally) and at least 5 occasions for everyone (paroxetine). CYP2D6 phenotype is given for 8 trials (mostly extensive metabolizers, 0 to 2 poor metabolizers per trial of 16; all 12 extensive in the paroxetine trial). No trial reported race or ethnicity (Discussion > Considerations for future research, 2nd paragraph).
sample.selection_effects: Search: one database, English only, publication-type filters, title or abstract terms; 30% of included publications came from hand selection that the paper does not describe, so the set cannot be reproduced from the stated strategy. Population: young, healthy, mostly ecstasy-naive adults screened for psychiatric illness, given the medicine once or for at most 14 days (Becker et al., 2021, for psilocybin); people who take these medicines because they have the conditions they treat, for months or years, were not studied. Two trials excluded people with high neuroticism scores and two admitted only people with previous ecstasy use (Discussion, 2nd paragraph).

exposure.measurement: As in each primary study: medicine and MDMA given in the laboratory, so doses and timing were known and the MDMA was laboratory-grade (Introduction > MDMA, 4th paragraph); blood levels were measured in some trials. Epidemiologic evidence rests on spontaneous reports to a surveillance database, a self-report survey and self-posted online accounts, with unverified drugs and doses.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only (Table 5): MDMA 75 to 125 mg by mouth once (or 1.5 or 1.6 mg/kg) after the medicine. Medicine conditions: citalopram 40 mg infused intravenously over 90 minutes; fluoxetine 20 mg daily for 5 to 11 days; paroxetine 20 mg daily for 3 days; duloxetine 120 mg at 16 and 4 hours before; reboxetine 8 mg at 12 and 1 hours before; bupropion XR raised to 300 mg over 7 days; methylphenidate 60 mg 1 hour before; haloperidol 1.4 mg intravenously; memantine 20 mg 2 hours before; carvedilol 50 mg, pindolol 20 mg and clonidine 0.15 mg 1 hour before; doxazosin 8 mg about 16 hours before after 3 days of run-in. Psilocybin trials used 0.17 to 0.25 mg/kg, or 25 mg.
exposure.polysubstance: Trials excluded active substance use. In the surveillance, survey and case-report data, other drugs and unverified MDMA content were the norm, and the review says drug levels could not be ascertained in most case reports (Discussion > Trends in case studies).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable at review level; trial washouts between sessions ranged from 2 days to 1 month (Table 5).

comparison.controls: Within each trial, the same people took placebo plus MDMA (and usually placebo plus placebo and medicine plus placebo), in counterbalanced order in most trials. Two designs differ: the paroxetine trial had only two sessions (paroxetine plus MDMA, placebo plus MDMA), and in the fluoxetine trial placebo pretreatment was always tested first (Table 5).
comparison.matching: Within-person crossover with washouts of 2 days to 1 month; no matching needed at trial level.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to the trials. For the surveillance, survey and case data, the reason for taking the medicine, its dose, duration and adherence are unknown, so the medicine cannot be separated from the illness or the circumstances.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable in the trials. In the surveillance data the comparison is with other reports in the same database.

outcomes.instruments: As in each primary study: plasma MDMA, MDA and HMMA (peak concentration, area under the curve, time to peak, half-life), heart rate, blood pressure, temperature, circulating catecholamines, pupil measures, visual analogue scales, Adjective Mood Rating Scale, 5-Dimensions of Altered States of Consciousness scale, Profile of Mood States, Addiction Research Center Inventory, List of Complaints and cognitive tasks; for the epidemiologic studies, a reported fatal outcome or reported adverse effects (Tables 5-7).
outcomes.operationalization: The review expresses each outcome as the percent change of (medicine plus MDMA) against (placebo plus MDMA) by one formula (Methods > Percent change calculation). Depending on the row the base is the peak effect (Emax), the peak change from baseline (delta Emax), the area under the effect curve, or a time-point value, and values marked with a tilde were estimated by the review's authors from graphs (Tables 6-7 footnotes).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None at review level. Significance marks (p<.05, p<.01, p<.001) are the primary studies' own, are not corrected for the many outcomes each trial measured, and are not shown for every row.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not assessed. Most trials are described as double-blind (Table 5); whether participants could tell a blunted from an unblunted MDMA session is not discussed.

analysis.effect_sizes: No pooled effect sizes and no intervals; only percent differences between two conditions (key findings). Editors' sum of Table 5: 193 participants across the 13 MDMA trials.
analysis.preregistration_detail: PROSPERO CRD42021233519 (Methods, 1st paragraph). The year in the identifier (2021) is later than the stated search date (21 December 2020), so the registration appears to follow the search; the registry record was not read, so the registered methods, including whether hand selection, case reports and epidemiologic studies were planned, are unchecked.
analysis.selective_reporting: All identified trials are tabulated, but secondary analyses of one sample are counted as separate publications. Percent changes are shown without the underlying means, so a reader cannot recompute them. The discussion stresses the consistent blunting by reuptake inhibitors and explains the exceptions (bupropion, doxazosin) by mechanism. The supplement with the case reports was not read.
analysis.power: Not applicable at review level. Included trials had 8 to 16 participants for MDMA (5 per group in one psilocybin study); the review does not discuss statistical power.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In single-dose or short-course laboratory trials in 8 to 16 healthy adults, pretreatment with an SSRI (citalopram, fluoxetine, paroxetine), an SNRI (duloxetine) or a noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor (reboxetine) lowered the effects of MDMA that people rated and that were measured (for example drug liking by about 31% with fluoxetine and about 62% with paroxetine, 'any drug effect' by about 62% with duloxetine and 21% with reboxetine), even though peak MDMA blood levels were 14 to 18% higher with paroxetine, duloxetine, reboxetine and bupropion. Bupropion was the exception: effects lasted longer and were not lower. Haloperidol turned MDMA's pleasant state dysphoric; methylphenidate added to heart rate and complaints without adding psychoactive effects; carvedilol cut heart-rate and temperature responses with little change in ratings; memantine changed nothing measured. There is no controlled study of MAOIs, benzodiazepines or lithium with MDMA; case reports (summary in a supplement not read) describe the worst outcomes with MAOIs; surveillance and survey data give associations that cannot separate the medicine from the circumstances.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract promises only a compilation. The conclusion says there are "clear acute pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic interactions" and then that the literature is not readily applicable to clinical settings. The discussion goes beyond the results in four places: it reads the lower heart rate, blood pressure and temperature responses as a reduced odds of serotonin syndrome (no trial measured serotonin toxicity); it says reuptake inhibitors outcompete MDMA at the transporters (tested only by an ex vivo binding measure in two trials); it proposes that blunted effects may lead people to take larger amounts and so explain the higher odds of death in the surveillance data (no included study tested this); and it says MAOIs cause dangerous serotonin elevations, resting on case reports. It also cites a pooled analysis of phase 2 trials (Feduccia et al., 2020), marked retracted in the PMC reference list, for the statement that people who had tapered antidepressants did worse.

timeline.event: de la Torre et al.: MDMA blood levels rise more than in proportion to dose, the background to the review's statement that MDMA inhibits its own breakdown
Schmid et al.: people with only non-functional CYP2D6 alleles reached higher MDMA levels (cited in the review's pharmacogenetics paragraph)
Cohen et al., surveillance-database analysis of co-ingested drugs and fatal outcomes in reports of ecstasy use, added by hand to this review after its search date
This review, the first systematic review of psychiatric-medicine interactions with MDMA or psilocybin by its authors' account; the only earlier review it names is narrative (Papaseit et al., 2020)

replication.where_it_stands: A compilation of controlled laboratory trials, mostly from one laboratory group by the review's own account (10 of the 13 MDMA trials carry Hysek, Liechti, Hasler or Schmid as first author in Table 5, editors' count), plus case reports and observational reports that only generate hypotheses. The consistent blunting by reuptake inhibitors rests on five trials with different first authors (Liechti, Tancer, Farre, Hysek) but small samples; the review does not establish their independence. The primary papers behind the key numbers (Liechti and Vollenweider 2000; Farre et al. 2007; Tancer and Johanson 2006; Hysek et al. 2011 and 2012; Schmid et al. 2015; Cohen et al. 2021) were not read for this card.

funding.funder: No funder for the review is named. Salary support for the last author came from the US Department of Veterans Affairs, Clinical Science Research and Development (award IK2CX001495); two people are thanked for assisting with abstract review (Acknowledgements).
funding.declared_conflicts: The last author has received payment from the MAPS Public Benefit Corporation for training clinicians in MDMA-assisted therapy; the third author runs a membership service that sells drug-interaction guides, courses and consultation; the other two authors declare none (Declarations).
funding.affiliations_note: The page text does not give affiliations. The reference list shows Thomas K. as last author of the surveillance study (Cohen et al., 2021) that the review added by hand, and the review's author list includes Kelan Thomas; whether they are the same person was not checked. The review cites the MAPS investigator's brochure for MDMA's dose range, onset and adverse effects.

what_would_settle_it: A supervised study of people who have taken an SSRI, SNRI or bupropion for months, given MDMA once with and without a washout of the medicine, with blood levels, CYP2D6 genotype, temperature and documented signs of serotonin toxicity measured, powered for safety outcomes rather than ratings; and a case registry of emergency presentations with toxicology that confirms the MDMA and records the medicine, its class and its duration. For MAOIs only systematic case collection with toxicology is ethical.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: PICOS stated: people of any age taking MDMA or psilocybin with a psychiatric medicine; comparison MDMA or psilocybin alone; outcomes in pharmacokinetics, physiology and subjective effects; study types listed (Methods, 1st paragraph).

A PROSPERO identifier is given, but its year (2021) is later than the stated search date (21 December 2020), the registry record was not read, the review has no risk-of-bias assessment that a protocol could have planned, and the 12 hand-selected records and the late additions are not reported as deviations.

Designs are listed, and the inclusion of epidemiologic studies despite their weaknesses (large samples, hypothesis generation) and of case reports in a supplement is explained (Study selection, 2nd paragraph).

One database (MEDLINE via PubMed), English only without justification, publication-type filters, title or abstract terms only, no grey literature, trial registries or reference-list searching described; 12 of 40 included publications (30%) were found outside the strategy, showing that it missed about a third; the search ended on 21 December 2020.
Each abstract was screened by two independent reviewers with disagreements settled by consensus; how full texts were assessed is not stated (Study selection, 1st paragraph).
How data were extracted and the percent changes computed, and by how many people, is not described.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Fig. 1 gives counts only (411 excluded on title or abstract, 16 on full text) with no list and no reasons; the supplement was not read.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 5 gives design, conditions, washout, sample size, sex, age, ecstasy experience and often CYP2D6 phenotype; Tables 6-7 give outcomes with timing. Setting, recruitment, funding and follow-up are not given, the epidemiologic studies are described in prose without group sizes or intervals, and the case reports are only in the supplement.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: None: neither the trials nor the observational studies were appraised.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported

domains.note: Narrative synthesis with percent changes; nothing pooled.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: Limits of generalizability are discussed (healthy volunteers, short exposure, unusual routes, Discussion, 2nd paragraph) and the case and epidemiologic data are called much less reliable (Introduction > MDMA, 4th paragraph), but without any appraisal the trial results are interpreted without reference to small samples, uncorrected multiple outcomes, the fixed order in one trial or unassessed blinding.

Differences between medicines are explained by mechanism only (bupropion, doxazosin); differences in route (intravenous citalopram), duration (one dose to 14 days), MDMA dose, sex mix and sample size are not related to the results, and paroxetine's larger cardiovascular effect is noted without explanation.
No quantitative synthesis; publication bias is not discussed. The authors contacted researchers with more than one trial for unpublished data and obtained none (Study selection, 2nd paragraph).

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Two authors' interests and the salary support are declared; no funding for the review itself is stated.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Five critical items are judged no (2, 4, 7, 9 and 13) and items 11 and 15 do not apply (no meta-analysis); more than one critical flaw gives critically low confidence under AMSTAR 2. This is a judgment about how far the review's summary can be trusted, not about the value of the trials it lists: the question is clear, the trial table is detailed and the review is candid that its evidence does not transfer to patients. The source can be cited for the list of medicines tested with MDMA in controlled settings, for the direction and approximate size (as computed by the review, without intervals) of what each primary trial found, and as a pointer to the primary papers. It should not be cited for precise effect sizes, for the safety or danger of any combination, for MAOI risk estimates, or for people taking medicines long-term. Where the review is the only source of a primary finding, claims should say 'as summarized by Sarparast et al. (2022)' and stay at draft until the primary paper is read.

key_findings.finding: 40 publications were included from 467 records screened (455 from MEDLINE via PubMed to 21 December 2020 plus 12 added by hand): 26 trial publications (17 original trials and 9 analyses of the same samples; 22 on MDMA, 4 on psilocybin), 3 epidemiologic studies and 11 case reports kept in a supplement; 411 records were excluded on title or abstract and 16 full texts on unstated grounds.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (Results); Methods > Search strategy, 1st paragraph; Study selection, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Fig. 1 (image, read on screen); Results, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: The 13 MDMA trials in Table 5 had 8 to 16 healthy adults each (editors' sum 193), nearly all double-blind counterbalanced crossovers; the medicine was given as a single dose or two doses within a day in 9 of the 13 and for 3 to 11 days in the other 4 (doxazosin, paroxetine, bupropion, fluoxetine); the longest pretreatment in any trial was 14 days (escitalopram, psilocybin). The fluoxetine trial always tested placebo pretreatment first, and the paroxetine trial had no placebo-only or paroxetine-only session. Authors state the trials were not designed for clinical extrapolation.

SSRIs lowered the rated and measured effects of MDMA. Citalopram (n=16): oceanic boundlessness about 60% lower, anxious ego dissolution about 63% lower (both p<.05), heart rate 12.3% lower at 60 minutes (p<.05), acute complaints about 46% lower (p<.01). Fluoxetine (n=8): drug liking 31.2%, 'high' 47.6% and 'stimulated' 40.1% lower (all p<.05), heart rate 14.6% lower (p<.05). Paroxetine (n=12): liking about 62%, 'high' about 68% (p<.001), systolic pressure about 41% (p<.001) and heart rate about 42% lower (p<.05). The review summarizes this as 30 to 80% lower subjective effects and 6 to 14% lower physiological effects, with paroxetine's physiological effect (40 to 60%) the exception. Values with a tilde were read off graphs by the review's authors.
key_findings.locator: Table 6, citalopram, fluoxetine and paroxetine rows; Results > MDMA > Serotonin reuptake inhibitors and MDMA, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: MDMA blood levels were higher with medicines that inhibit CYP2D6 or related enzymes, at the same time as effects were lower. Paroxetine: peak +16.0% and exposure to 21 hours +21.6% (both p<.01), with the main metabolite HMMA 49.3% lower at peak. Duloxetine: peak +14.6%, exposure to 6 hours +16.2%, HMMA peak 40.5% lower. Reboxetine: peak +17.8%, exposure to 24 hours +8.1% (p<.05). Bupropion: peak +14.3%, exposure to 24 hours +33.1% (p<.001), HMMA peak 75.9% lower. Carvedilol (+4.7%), clonidine (-2.9%), doxazosin (-1.6%), methylphenidate (-3.5%) and memantine (-1.0% at 1 hour) changed the peak by 5% or less. Table 6 has no blood-level row for citalopram or fluoxetine.
key_findings.locator: Table 6, pharmacokinetic rows (Cmax, AUC) for each medicine; Results > MDMA, the paragraphs on bupropion, serotonin reuptake inhibitors, duloxetine and reboxetine

key_findings.finding: Duloxetine (n=16) lowered nearly every effect of MDMA: 'any drug effect' 61.7%, drug liking 57.7% and closeness to others 83.1% (all p<.001), heart rate 57.4% and systolic pressure 63.5% (p<.001), and acute complaints 122.5% (p<.01; above 100% because the base is a change from baseline). Reboxetine (n=16) lowered 'any drug effect' by 20.7% (p<.01), closeness by 38.6% (p<.05), heart rate by 26.2% (p<.05) and systolic pressure by 46.5% (p<.001), but drug liking (-10.0%) and good drug effect (-15.2%) did not change significantly.
key_findings.locator: Table 6, duloxetine and reboxetine rows; Results > MDMA > Serotonin reuptake inhibitors and MDMA, 2nd paragraph; Reboxetine and MDMA

key_findings.finding: Bupropion XR (n=16) did not blunt the rated effects: peak ratings of any drug effect, good effect, 'high' and liking were 5.6 to 17.1% higher (no significance marks) and the areas under their curves over 8 hours were 34.0 to 46.1% higher (p<.05 for any drug effect, good effect, 'high' and liking), meaning the effects lasted longer, while heart rate was 38.7% lower (p<.001) and norepinephrine 65.6% lower (p<.05).
key_findings.locator: Table 6, bupropion rows (Physiological; Circulating catecholamines; Subjective); Results > MDMA > Bupropion and MDMA

key_findings.finding: Haloperidol 1.4 mg intravenously (n=14) did not change heart rate, blood pressure or temperature responses to MDMA but made the state dysphoric: well-being about 31% lower (p<.05), state anxiety about 47% higher at 75 minutes (p<.01), oceanic boundlessness about 59% lower (p<.05).
key_findings.locator: Table 6, haloperidol rows; Results > MDMA > Antipsychotics and MDMA

key_findings.finding: Methylphenidate (n=16) delayed MDMA's time to peak by 45.8% (p<.05) without changing its peak (-3.5%) or exposure (+3.2%), raised heart rate 15.1% and the rate-pressure product 16.8% (both p<.001) and epinephrine 54.6% (p<.01), and raised acute and subacute complaints by 86.5% (p<.01) and 191.9% (p<.001), without adding psychoactive effects (any drug effect -1.4%).
key_findings.locator: Table 6, methylphenidate rows; Results > MDMA > Psychostimulants and MDMA

key_findings.finding: Adrenergic agents (n=16 each unless stated): carvedilol lowered the heart-rate rise 79.0%, systolic 76.9% (both p<.001), diastolic 39.2% and temperature 42.0% (p<.05) with little change in ratings (any drug effect +7.4%, liking +1.5%) while epinephrine and norepinephrine rose; pindolol (n=16, men) lowered peak heart rate about 17.6% (p<.001) and 'dreaminess'; clonidine lowered mean arterial pressure and norepinephrine; doxazosin lowered mean arterial pressure 6.8% (p<.05) but raised heart rate 9.6% (p<.05) and lowered heightened-mood ratings. Carvedilol and doxazosin percentages are changes from baseline, pindolol's is on the raw peak.
key_findings.locator: Table 6, adrenergic-agent rows (carvedilol, pindolol, clonidine, doxazosin); Results > MDMA > Adrenergic agents and MDMA, 2nd to 5th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Memantine 20 mg (n=15) had no effect on MDMA-induced memory impairment or on mood, per the review; Table 6 lists changes of 0.8 to 41.1% on memory and mood measures without significance marks.
key_findings.locator: Table 6, memantine rows; Results > MDMA > Memantine and MDMA

key_findings.finding: Psilocybin: escitalopram taken for 14 days (n=23) did not significantly lower altered-states ratings (oceanic boundlessness unchanged; anxious ego dissolution -40%, visionary restructuralization -4.7%) but lowered bad drug effects 53.8% (p<.01), fear 50% (p<.01) and systolic pressure 43.8% (p<.001) and left psilocin levels unchanged (+1.0%); buspirone lowered visionary restructuralization by about 44% (p<.001); risperidone 1 mg by about 27% (p<.01); haloperidol raised dread of ego dissolution by about 27% (p<.05); ergotamine had no effect on subjective ratings.
key_findings.locator: Table 7; Results > Psilocybin (antipsychotics, serotonin agonists, serotonin reuptake inhibitors)

key_findings.finding: The 11 case reports are summarized only in a supplement (not read). The main text says the highest rates of morbidity came from MDMA with MAOIs such as moclobemide or phenelzine, with hyperthermia, seizure-like activity and altered mental state suggestive of serotonin syndrome, many ending in death; coronary artery disease was found at autopsy in several; one young man with bipolar disorder who took moclobemide and lithium was left unaccompanied for 4 hours and found dead; drug levels were unknown in most. SSRI cases were described as consistent with blunted effects. The main text gives no count of cases or deaths per drug. No controlled study of MAOIs, benzodiazepines or lithium with MDMA was found.
key_findings.locator: Discussion > Trends in case studies, 1st paragraph; Discussion > MDMA psychopharmacology > Pharmacodynamic interactions, 3rd paragraph; Discussion > Considerations for future research, 3rd paragraph; Table 4

key_findings.finding: Surveillance study (Cohen et al., 2021, as summarized here): 946 unique reports of recreational ecstasy use in the US adverse-event database, 2000-2020 (mean age 28, 70.1% men). Adjusted odds ratios of a fatal outcome when a drug class was also reported: benzodiazepines 2.25, opioids 2.05, ethanol 2.03, amphetamines and stimulants 3.05, antidepressants 1.62. Unadjusted odds ratios for single psychiatric medicines: bupropion 2.82, sertraline 2.36, venlafaxine 1.97, citalopram 1.92, olanzapine 1.86; all 18 reports with metoclopramide ended in death; no deaths were reported with risperidone or lithium. No intervals, numbers of deaths or denominators are given.

Survey (Copeland et al., 2006, as summarized here): 216 adults who took ecstasy with a pharmaceutical drug in the past 6 months (mean age 26, 63% men, mean 11 days of ecstasy use in 6 months). Of those who took antidepressants with ecstasy, 76% still felt euphoria, but rates of muscle rigidity (0% vs 45%), nystagmus (0% vs 33%), dizziness (19% vs 42%), headache (21% vs 62%) and heavy sweating (28% vs 53%) were higher; antidepressants were not analysed by class and included MAOIs. Group sizes and the order of the paired percentages are not stated.

Pharmacogenetics and metabolism, second-hand: MDMA is cleared mainly by CYP2D6 to the inactive metabolite HMMA and is thought to inhibit CYP2D6 itself, giving non-linear kinetics; people with only non-functional alleles (*3, *4, *5) had a peak MDMA level 19% higher and early exposure (to 6 hours) 25% higher than people with only *1 and *2 alleles, with faster onset and higher blood pressure (Schmid et al., 2016); pooled trial data show effects follow plasma concentration and higher CYP2D6 activity scores predict lower MDMA levels (Studerus et al., 2021). The review names the strong enzyme blocker ritonavir as having caused significant toxicity with MDMA (Papaseit et al., 2012).
key_findings.locator: Introduction > MDMA, 2nd paragraph; Discussion > Pharmacokinetic interactions, 1st paragraph; Discussion > Pharmacogenetics and MDMA, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: No trial gave an SSRI or SNRI for months in people who take one as treatment; the longest pretreatment was 14 days (escitalopram, psilocybin trial) and for MDMA 5 to 11 days (fluoxetine). The authors state that modern MDMA-therapy trials either excluded people taking psychiatric medicines or stopped them first, and that none of the psilocybin trials measured physiology.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 2nd paragraph; Discussion > Considerations for future research, 1st paragraph; Table 5

reporting_issues.issue: The text says the 12 hand-selected articles arose while reading full texts, but Fig. 1 adds them at identification (467 records screened by title and abstract); the 16 full-text exclusions have no reasons in the figure or text.
reporting_issues.consequence: The route by which 30% of the included publications entered is unclear and cannot be reproduced; any claim from this review should be treated as resting on a selected, not an exhaustive, body of evidence.

reporting_issues.issue: Results say plasma MDMA concentrations rose with both fluoxetine and paroxetine, but Table 6 has pharmacokinetic rows only for paroxetine among the SSRIs, none for fluoxetine or citalopram.
reporting_issues.consequence: A rise in MDMA levels is shown for paroxetine, duloxetine, reboxetine and bupropion only; the statement for fluoxetine is not supported by anything tabulated.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says bupropion did affect self-reported complaints from MDMA, but Table 6 lists changes of -5.0% (acute) and -6.0% (subacute) with no significance marks, and the same paragraph then says bupropion prolonged positive mood.
reporting_issues.consequence: One of the two statements is probably misworded (the table supports 'did not significantly affect'); the complaints finding should not be cited.

reporting_issues.issue: Percent changes in Tables 6 and 7 mix bases: peak effect, peak change from baseline, area under the effect curve, single time points and graph-read estimates, with no means, SDs, n per outcome or intervals; changes beyond 100% appear (norepinephrine -143.2% with duloxetine and -109.8% with clonidine; acute complaints -122.5% with duloxetine).
reporting_issues.consequence: Sizes in different rows are not comparable (a 79.0% fall in carvedilol's heart-rate change against a 17.6% fall in pindolol's heart-rate peak), none has an interval, and a figure above 100% means the effect reversed, not that it was removed twice.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 5 states that placebo pretreatment was always tested first in the fluoxetine trial, and the paroxetine trial had two sessions only, yet both are counted among the 26 randomized controlled studies; the 1967 chlorpromazine and 1998 psilocybin trials are described only as placebo-controlled crossovers.
reporting_issues.consequence: Randomization and counterbalancing are overstated for two of the three SSRI trials with subjective outcomes; order and expectancy are confounded with the medicine in the fluoxetine result.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion reads lower heart rate, blood pressure and temperature responses as a reduced odds of serotonin syndrome and says blunted effects may drive larger amounts and the higher odds of death for antidepressant combinations in the surveillance data; no included study measured serotonin toxicity or the amount taken, and the same review reports adjusted odds of death of 1.62 with antidepressants and unadjusted 2.36 with sertraline and 2.82 with bupropion.
reporting_issues.consequence: Both statements are hypotheses; neither reassurance nor alarm follows from the trials, and the surveillance odds ratios (spontaneous reports, no denominators) cannot show that any antidepressant raises the risk of death.

reporting_issues.issue: The review describes several antidepressant-plus-MDMA combinations as having increased mortality, from odds ratios in a spontaneous-report database.
reporting_issues.consequence: A causal verb is used for a reporting association without denominators, intervals or knowledge of dose, purity or indication.

reporting_issues.issue: Feduccia et al. (2020), marked retracted in the PMC reference list, is cited for reduced efficacy of MDMA-assisted therapy after recent tapering of reuptake inhibitors, including 63.6% against 25.0% still meeting PTSD criteria.
reporting_issues.consequence: A retracted paper is read as a record of what was claimed, never as evidence (METHODS 3.2); the statements that rest on it are not used by any claim built from this card.

reporting_issues.issue: The text gives the range of sample sizes as 8 to 23 and Table 5 gives 5 for each of the two haloperidol and risperidone psilocybin groups, with 7 women and 8 men listed for the two groups together; Hysek et al. 2012b, cited in the Results among trials with adrenergic agents, is a study of MDMA and emotion recognition and is not in Table 5; the Table 6 footnote expands SERT as 'sertraline transporter'.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor: the psilocybin samples are smaller than stated, one citation is wrong and one abbreviation is mis-expanded (serotonin transporter); none changes an MDMA result.

reporting_issues.issue: The survey summary gives pairs of percentages (for example headache 21% vs 62%) without saying which group each belongs to or how many people took antidepressants; the surveillance summary gives no intervals, counts of deaths or denominators.
reporting_issues.consequence: Neither study's figures can be turned into absolute risks or checked for chance; they can only be quoted as reported by the review.
